system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- Evidence text comes from a PDF text layer. If symbols are garbled so that you cannot verify the atom, answer "hold" for that check and say so.
- Be strict. When unsure between pass and a non-pass value, choose the non-pass value and explain.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom. pass = fully stated. revise = the core claim is stated, and the gap is only wording, strength, or a dropped/extra peripheral qualifier that can be fixed by deleting or softening words (say what). fail = not stated, OR the atom adds substantive content the evidence lacks: a scope or population restriction (e.g. 'In B-ALL'), a mechanism or operation, a characterization (e.g. 'an unbounded while loop'), or a formula/definition. If deleting the unsupported part would change what the atom tests, it is fail, not revise. For pass, put the supporting evidence ids in cite (required).
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / revise / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge: one fact a person who studied the concept would simply know. revise = the core fact is recall-level but the sentence carries extra load that must be removed, e.g. stacked conditions (since/although/if ... and ...), a procedural or evaluative add-on ('easy to define but requires checking ...'), or a clause that introduces a second technical concept that must be known separately (e.g. 'if X is an inner Kan complex' when that is not the card concept). fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = the authors' opinion or choice, or the finding of one study, so the answer is not fixed without the source.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a single system, product, or one study's topic.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Deresuscitation
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Active removal of accumulated fluid: definitions (LCFM, LGFR), rationale, monitoring of hypervolemia, diuretic/albumin/ultrafiltration strategies, safety stop criteria, and evidence limits. Excludes IAH-specific management.

ATOMS:
- IVFLUID-C08-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Late Goal-Directed Fluid Removal (LGFR), also called de-resuscitation, is defined as active fluid removal with diuretics or renal replacement therapy with net ultrafiltration, started within the first week of ICU stay.
  EVIDENCE:
    [IVFLUID-p0207-s18] Definitions and Key Messages • Late Goal-Directed Fluid Removal (LGFR) is defined as active fluid removal
    [IVFLUID-p0207-s19] with diuretics or renal replacement therapy with net ultrafiltration and started within the first week of ICU stay also referred to as de-resuscitation
- IVFLUID-C08-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Late Conservative Fluid Management (LCFM) is defined as 2 consecutive days of negative fluid balance within the first week of the ICU stay, and describes a moderate fluid management strategy after the initial early adequate fluid management to avoid or reverse fluid overload.
  EVIDENCE:
    [IVFLUID-p0207-s02] Late Conservative Fluid Management (LCFM) describes a moderate fluid management strategy following the initial EAFM in order to avoid (or reverse) fluid overload.
    [IVFLUID-p0207-s15] Definitions and Key Messages • Late Conservative Fluid Management (LCFM) is defined as 2 consecutive days
    [IVFLUID-p0207-s16] of negative fluid balance within the first week of the ICU stay.
- IVFLUID-C08-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: De-resuscitation is defined as a strategy of actively and forcefully removing accumulated fluid, in an otherwise hemodynamically stable patient with clinical evidence of fluid overload, in order to treat or prevent end-organ damage from fluid overload without producing hypovolemia and organ ischemia.
  EVIDENCE:
    [IVFLUID-p0516-s18] De-resuscitate when necessary: De-resuscitation is a strategy to remove accu­
    [IVFLUID-p0516-s19] mulated fluid forcefully, in an otherwise hemodynamically stable patient with clinical evidence of fluid overload.
    [IVFLUID-p0516-s20] The aim of de-resuscitation is to treat and/or prevent end-organ damage resulting from fluid overload without producing hypovolemia and organ ischemia.
- IVFLUID-C08-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: In a randomized trial of hemodynamically stable, hypoproteinemic mechanically ventilated ARDS patients, adding 20% albumin boluses to furosemide for 72 hours produced a larger negative fluid balance, fewer hypotension episodes and significantly improved oxygenation compared with furosemide plus placebo.
  EVIDENCE:
    [IVFLUID-p0517-s17] In an elegant study, Greg Martin et al. randomized hemodynamically stable, hypoproteinemic patients who are on mechanical ventilator for ARDS to either furosemide with albumin (100 ml boluses of 20% albumin every 8-h) or furosemide with placebo for 72 h [16].
    [IVFLUID-p0517-s18] Addition of albumin was shown to produce larger negative fluid balance and lesser episodes of hypotension, in addition to a significant improvement in oxygenation.
- IVFLUID-C08-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: The PAL strategy (PEEP matched to intra-abdominal pressure, plus albumin, plus furosemide or ultrafiltration) was associated, in a pilot study, with greater negative fluid balance and greater reduction in extravascular lung water index and intra-abdominal pressure than in control subjects, with improved oxygenation and shorter ICU stay and without compromising cardiovascular or renal function.
  EVIDENCE:
    [IVFLUID-p0517-s20] –– Addition of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) matching intra-abdomi­
    [IVFLUID-p0517-s21] nal pressure (IAP), in addition to albumin plus diuretics (or ultrafiltration) (PAL strategy—PEEP, albumin and lasix or furosemide), had shown to be associated with greater negative fluid balance and greater reduction in extravascular lung water index (EVLWI) and IAP compared to control subjects [17].
    [IVFLUID-p0517-s22] PAL strategy also showed improved clinical outcomes (improved oxygenation, shorter ICU length of stay) without compromising cardiovascular or renal function.
- IVFLUID-C08-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: Active fluid removal in de-resuscitation can be achieved either by judicious use of diuretics or by ultrafiltration using continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) or slow low efficiency hemodialysis (SLED).
  EVIDENCE:
    [IVFLUID-p0517-s01] • How to initiate? Active removal of fluid can be achieved either by judicious use
    [IVFLUID-p0517-s02] of diuretics or by ultrafiltration [continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) or slow low efficiency hemodialysis (SLED)].
- IVFLUID-C08-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: De-resuscitation should be stopped when hemodynamic instability or obvious hypovolemia occurs, in which case fluid removal is suspended and fluid may be judiciously re-administered, and removal may be restarted at a lower rate once hypovolemia or hypoperfusion is mitigated.
  EVIDENCE:
    [IVFLUID-p0518-s10] –– Hemodynamic instability or obvious evidence of hypovolemia; in which case,
    [IVFLUID-p0518-s11] fluid removal must be suspended and fluid may be re-administered judiciously.
    [IVFLUID-p0518-s12] Fluid removal may be re-initiated at a lower rate, once hypovolemia or hypoperfusion is mitigated [12].
- IVFLUID-C08-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: De-resuscitation should be considered only when the patient is hemodynamically stable on no or minimal vasopressor dose, needs no additional fluid boluses and has no ongoing fluid loss requiring replacement, and has clinical and objective evidence of fluid overload with reasonable suspicion of organ damage directly resulting from fluid accumulation.
  EVIDENCE:
    [IVFLUID-p0516-s22] • When to start? Patient must be hemodynamically stable on no or minimal dose
    [IVFLUID-p0516-s23] of vasopressors before considering de-resuscitation.
    [IVFLUID-p0516-s24] He or she should not be requiring additional boluses or fluid or there should not be any ongoing fluid loss requiring replacement.
    [IVFLUID-p0516-s25] Clinical and objective evidence of fluid overload should be present with reasonable suspicion of organ damage (or impending one) directly resulting from the fluid accumulation.
- IVFLUID-C08-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: De-resuscitation is an active fluid removal to treat fluid accumulation causing organ dysfunction, whereas de-escalation means discontinuing or reducing IV fluids to prevent fluid accumulation.
  EVIDENCE:
    [IVFLUID-p0515-s09] De-escalation means discontinuation or reducing IV fluids to prevent fluid accumulation.
    [IVFLUID-p0515-s10] De-resuscitation is an active fluid removal to treat fluid accumulation causing organ dysfunction.
